documentation.range:
Muskoxen currently have a circum-arctic distribution, having been reintroduced to regions that they had disappeared from historically (Alaska) and pre-historically (Russia). Muskoxen occur naturally on Northeast and North Greenland. In Canada, endemic Muskoxen have mostly reoccupied the mainland ranges, which were severely contracted at the end of the 19th century due to commercial harvesting. The species occupies the mainland tundra from the coast of Hudson Bay west to almost the Mackenzie River and south to the tree line. However, distribution is discontinuous: waves of recolonization have spread out from refugia and gaps in distribution appear behind the colonizing edges. Muskoxen are distributed across all the Canadian Arctic Islands, except the eastern Arctic islands of Baffin and islands in Hudson Bay.

In Russia, Muskoxen were successfully reintroduced to the Taimyr Peninsula and subsequently to ten other sites along the north coast. In Alaska, Muskoxen were reintroduced to found several populations, which have a discontinuous distribution across the northwestern and northern coastal plan and have dispersed into Canada’s Yukon Territory. Muskoxen were introduced and are well established in West Greenland. The introduction to Norway included a few Muskoxen which dispersed into Sweden. Muskoxen are not found on the Eurasian Arctic Islands, except for an introduction to Wrangel Island in 1975 and unsuccessful introductions to Svalbard (1929–1985) and Iceland (1929–1932).

The Alaskan, Yukon (dispersed from Alaska) and Russian reintroductions are within the natural range as Muskoxen from Alaska disappeared by the 1890s and from Russia about 2,000 years ago and were subsequently reintroduced 1935 and 1974, respectively. The 1962–1963 introductions to west Greenland were introduced in case of an exceptionally severe winter threatening the endemic Muskoxen on east Greenland (Lent 1999). Lack of fossil evidence means that this assessment does not include the Muskoxen introduced to Canada’s Ungava Peninsula in 1967 (to establish a knitting industry based on wool) or the introductions to Norway and Sweden (Lent 1999).
documentation.population:
Globally, the three-generation global trend is an 8% decrease from approximately 157,100 Muskoxen indexed in 1998 to 127,102 by 2019 (Table 1 in the Supplementary Information). The assessment draws on the collaborative work undertaken through the Muskox Expert Network (MOXNET) established through the Arctic Council’s Circumpolar Biodiversity Monitoring Program (Cuyler et al. 2020).

Recent collapses on the Canadian Banks and Victoria islands (1996–2019) have skewed the overall trends, despite increasing Muskox numbers for the reintroductions in Russia, Alaska and west Greenland. Numbers of northeast Greenland’s endemic Muskoxen are unknown since the early 1990s except for one area where Muskoxen declined in the last decade (Schmidt et al. 2015). The greatest uncertainty for the estimated numbers is the irregular frequency of surveys and changes in the boundaries of survey areas (Cuyler et al. 2020).

The endemic Canadian Muskoxen had been seen as a conservation success story (Barr 1991). Unregulated commercial harvesting on the continental mainland in the late 1800s left only a handful of Muskoxen in scattered areas by the 1930s, and the species had almost disappeared from the larger arctic islands after severe winters. Subsequently, with tightly regulated hunting, Muskox abundance rebounded (Barr 1991). But recently, within the three-generation time span, regional trends have sharply diverged between the islands and continental mainland. For example, Banks and Victoria islands in the mid-1990s had 87,800 Muskoxen, which were 61% of Canada’s Muskoxen, but by 2019, the population had declined 47% to 16,480, which is now 21% of Canada’s Muskoxen population. The endemic Muskoxen in Canada are monitored in 30 survey areas and by 2019, totalled about 79,580 Muskoxen which had reoccupied their historic range on the continental mainland. However, behind the dispersing fronts, Muskox abundance declines, which has also been seen in Alaska (Cuyler et al. 2020). Muskoxen on the Canada’s High Arctic Islands fluctuate with long recoveries following abrupt declines during winter with unusually severe icing and late melting snow. A similar pattern appears to hold for northeast Greenland. For example, the Zackenberg Muskoxen slowly increased 1996 to 2007 then declined (Schmidt et al. 2015, 2019) and recovery may be slow after even ‘small’ perturbations (Desforges et al. 2021). Alaskan Muskoxen increased and spread and by 2018, are in six regions where the population totalled 3,700. Trends among the regions vary, with peaks in abundance coinciding with emigration (Reynolds 1998) and declines from complex causes (Afema et al. 2017). The reintroductions to Russia started in 1974 and 1975 with 10 Muskoxen from Canada and 40 Muskoxen from Alaska, to Taimyr Peninsula and Wrangel Island, respectively. The reintroduced Muskoxen increased in number and were then translocated to eight more regions on the Russian mainland tundra and two areas were naturally colonised (Cuyler et al. 2020).
documentation.habitats:
Muskoxen are the largest herbivore found on the tundra, which extends from the limits of plant growth on the High Arctic Islands and northern Greenland to the continental mainland. In Canada, muskoxen are found south to within the tree line zone where the boreal forest meets the tundra.

Muskox ecology is dominated by a short and variable plant growing season (when diet quality is high) and a long winter when the availability of low-quality forage is highly variable through snow cover (Barboza and Reynolds 2004). Although primarily grazers adapted to a diet of sedges and grasses, Muskoxen also browse shrubs and forage selectively for forbs. Muskoxen have a high nutrient intake in the late summer, as they concentrate much of their fat and protein gain into 4–6 weeks. Muskoxen have a high threshold of fat reserves before conceiving, which reflects their conservative breeding strategies (Adamczewski et al. 1992) and they calve well before snow melt, so lactation is supported by the cow’s fat reserves. Winter ranges typically have shallow snow to reduce the energetic costs of digging through snow to reach forage. Muskoxen live in mixed sex and age herds or small male bachelor herds and typically seasonally move within  home ranges (Gunn and Adamczewski 2003).

Muskox predators include wolves, grizzly bears and rarely, polar bears (Tener 1965). In Alaska and western Canada, based on radio-collared Muskoxen, predation was likely a factor in muskox declines through interactions with disease and parasites (Arthur and Del Vecchio 2017, Afema et al. 2016). Accidents include Muskoxen either becoming marooned on islands in lakes as ice breaks up or breaking through thin lake ice and drowning, as was recorded in Alaska (Lenart 2015). When freezing rain has led to forage unavailability in early winter, muskoxen have moved onto the sea ice and died (Patten 1997).
documentation.threats:
The arctic is rapidly warming, but understanding Muskox sensitivity to a warmer climate is only just beginning. Effects will include interacting factors such as a cascade of effects on forage quality and quantity including levels of micro-nutrients such as copper, which is essential for immune function, and low copper levels have been implicated in Muskox health (Afema et al. 2017). Warmer falls with rain and icing or deeper snow are a concern as Muskoxen depend on fall foraging and access to lowland habitats (Tomassini et al. 2019). A warmer climate is also changing Muskox exposure to diseases and parasites, as the parasites and disease vectors are also responding to a warmer climate (Kaffle et al. 2020). Hotter summers with heat stress coincided with recent outbreaks of Erysipelas on Banks Island (Kutz et al. 2015). A potential threat is novel diseases especially as Muskoxen have low genetic variability (Prewer et al. 2019) although the implications of low genetic variability for immune function are complex (Sommers 2005) and not yet described for Muskoxen.

Habitat changes in the Arctic are relatively small scale and local habitat alterations due to roads, mines and oil and gas explorations and developments. In North America and Greenland, local communities have a voice in monitoring and mitigation of effects of industrial developments.
documentation.measures:
Re-introductions have reduced muskox global vulnerabilities, as muskoxen are now distributed on a circum-arctic scale. The initial stages of re-colonization are increasing abundance and dispersal but then followed by declines and less is known about the longer-term trends. The return of Muskoxen to areas not occupied in living memory of local communities can cause local concerns, especially for whether Muskoxen negatively affect caribou abundance.

In the US, muskoxen occur in five protected areas and in Greenland, Muskoxen are in four protected areas, with indigenous populations in the vast Northeast Greenland National Park, and three introduced populations in Arnangarnup Qoorua Nature Reserve, and Kangerlussuag and Maniitsoq Caribou Reserves. Canada does not have reserves specifically set aside for Muskoxen, but part of the rationale for establishing the Thelon Game Sanctuary was to protect a remnant Muskox population from hunting. The species also occurs in three national parks: Quttinirpaaq (Ellesmere Island), Aulavik (northern Banks Island) and Tuktu Nogait (Bluenose Lake, western Arctic mainland). In national parks, land use activities are controlled, but aboriginal hunting is permitted subject to conservation provisions.
documentation.use_trade: Muskox hunting has been part of Aboriginal culture for thousands of years and is still important to Inuit communities for meat and hides; the horns are valued for local handicrafts and a luxury market exists for qivuit, the remarkably fine underwool (Lent 1999, Tomascelli et al. 2018, Cuyler et al. 2019). Muskox hunting is typically regulated through quotas in Alaska, Canada and Greenland and licensed sport-hunting contributes to community economies. Illegal hunting is infrequent.
documentation.rationale: Muskoxen are listed as Least Concern in view of their wide distribution, presumed large populations, and because their overall rate of change over three generations is less than required to qualify for listing in a threatened category.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The question of subspecies is uncertain and in the absence of updated taxonomic studies with more recent techniques, this assessment reflects the Tener’s (1963) conclusions. Tener (1963) used morphological skull measurements and examination of pelage and body size characteristics to conclude the sub-speciation was incipient and thus there was no basis to recognize the subspecies Ovibos moschatus moschatus and O. m. wardi. A study of mtDNA also did not support the two subspecies (Groves 1997).
